title: Wisdom, Courage, and Honest Living
overview: This chapter collects short sayings that set the lasting rewards of wisdom, fairness and hard work against the quick gains and sudden end of wrongdoing.

parts.label: Envy versus wisdom (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: People who get ahead by violence may look enviable, but wisdom builds a household (family as well as home) that lasts, and good advice wins battles better than force. A fool has nothing to say at the city gate, where elders settled public matters, and anyone who plots harm earns the name of schemer.

parts.label: Rescue the condemned (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Hard times show how much strength a person really has. The reader is told to step in for those being unjustly led to death, and pleading ignorance does not fool God, who weighs the heart.

parts.label: Wisdom is sweet (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: As honey tastes good, wisdom is good for a person and gives a future worth hoping for. Seven times here means many times: good people may fall often but get back up, while wrongdoers are brought down by disaster.

parts.label: No gloating, no fretting (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: Do not celebrate an enemy's fall, since God dislikes that spirit and may ease off punishing them; scholars debate the exact sense, but the warning against gloating is clear. Do not stew over evil people, whose lamp, meaning their life and prosperity, will go out, and respect the LORD and the king rather than joining officials bent on overthrowing order.

parts.label: Fair courts, honest words (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: A new small collection warns judges against favoring anyone, calls an honest answer as welcome as a kiss, and advises securing your living in the fields before building a home. It also forbids false testimony and paying people back in kind, a line Christians often read alongside Jesus' teaching against revenge.

parts.label: The overgrown field (vv. 30-34)
parts.note: The writer walks past a lazy man's land, choked with thorns and weeds, its stone wall collapsed. The lesson is that small, repeated bits of putting things off add up, and poverty arrives as suddenly as a robber.

think: When someone who has wronged you suffers a setback, what do you notice happening inside you?
